extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary critics, and informed readers interested in standards for poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive principles for composing and judging poetry and drama (verse harmony, dramatic probability, character-ideal balance, translation fidelity, theatrical programming). Aimed at guiding writers, translators, critics, and theatre managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious verse (arrangement of pauses and cadences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonious verse consists in 'the apt arrangement of pauses and cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs,' and not in 'the even flow, much less in the prominence of antithetic vigour, of single lines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: English iambic blank verse excels by long-linked sweetness ('with many a winding bout / Of linked sweetness long drawn out'). Single-line epigrams or violent antitheses are 'injurious to the total effect' except when purposely introduced for a specific effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity and faithfulness to the original
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations must be faithful to the original text; bad translations may add pages not in the original or omit large portions ('the English was no translation--there were pages on pages not in the original--and half the original was not to be found in the translation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique translations that invent or omit material; aim for fidelity in content and spirit. Beware of translations that distort the author's intent or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect native idiom and language spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Each language has its particular spirit and genius; translators and writers should not 'sacrifice' the idiom of the target language to the original ('Voss... had done violence to the idiom of the Germans, and had sacrificed it to the Greeks').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid crude literalism or excessive foreign idioms. Coleridge warns that Milton sometimes injured his English by borrowing idioms; borrowing is 'a very dangerous practice.' Prefer clarity and native idiomatic usage in prose and verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-for-line equivalence caution in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Klopstock's claim: 'a German line proved always sufficient for a Greek or Latin one. In English you cannot do this.' Coleridge replies that English often renders a Greek heroic line in a line and a half.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious claiming one-to-one correspondence of metrical lines across languages; expect differences in tempo, syllable-count, and idiomatic expansion when rendering classics into English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a deliberate plan/structure in long poems and odes
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should attend to the plan of their odes/poems; Klopstock 'values himself upon the plan of his odes, and accuses the modern lyrical writers of gross deficiency in this respect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A carefully conceived plan (even if its execution is episodic) distinguishes lasting works; avoid loosely assembled or merely episodic verse. Coleridge notes long composition cycles where planning preceded sustained composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's moral/educative aim: raise the audience, do not descend to them
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet should 'raise people up to his own level, not to descend to theirs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pandering to popular taste by lowering standards; artists ought to elevate readers/viewers intellectually and morally rather than merely gratifying base appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on mere animal gratification as chief interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Oberon: 'it was unworthy of a man of genius to make the interest of a long poem turn entirely upon animal gratification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romantic or erotic appeals may please many, but making sensual appetite the dominant engine of a long work is viewed as trivial or cheap art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability achieved through harmony of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when characters and incidents 'border on impossibility,' a poet can achieve 'dramatic probability' sufficient for pleasure if 'the whole of his work be in harmony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension of disbelief is acceptable provided internal coherence and tonal/harmonic unity; the poet 'solicits us only to yield ourselves to a dream'—the work must sustain that dream consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal art: balance of the generic and the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of ideal art is 'the happy balance of the generic with the individual' — the generic makes a character representative and instructive, the individual gives living interest and reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid figures that are mere abstractions or mere portraits; strive for characters that simultaneously symbolize broader types and remain concretely individual and vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character intelligibility and representative power
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful dramatic/poetic character (e.g., Don Juan, Satan in Paradise Lost) is intelligible as a type and capable of interesting 'without poetry, nay, even without words' due to idealized compositional balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters whose motives and actions are immediately comprehensible as representative types while retaining distinctive individuality that secures audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overuse extravagant gothic/horrific incident as substitute for true imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called German drama (and imitators) often employed 'ruined castles, the dungeons, the trap-doors, the skeletons, the flesh-and-blood ghosts, and the perpetual moonshine'—an 'olla podrida' that critics called 'cramps of weakness' and 'orgasms of a sickly imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid piling sensational or Gothic tropes as a substitute for genuine poetic invention; such tropes can signal weakness of taste and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap sentimental manipulation (easy tears)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge: 'nothing was more easy than to deluge an audience, that it was done every day by the meanest writers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on contrived sentimentality to elicit tears; seek authentic emotional truth and depth rather than mechanical devices to manipulate audience emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (intellectual or social) as dramatic/poetic desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Without power, virtue would be insufficient and incapable of revealing its being; 'hence power is necessarily an object of our desire and of our admiration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character and theme, depict power (of mind, status, etc.) when needed to reveal moral qualities; the contrast of intellectual lordship with guilt yields strong dramatic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/comparative analysis in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand a literary phenomenon, compare it with an elder production whose likeness is striking yet whose real differences illuminate the new work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply comparative critique (e.g., comparing Don Juan with Atheista Fulminato or German drama with earlier English/Spanish models) to reveal origins, influences, and departures; this aids clear insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre-management criterion for artistic restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers entrusted to 'redeem' the stage should possess 'rank, fortune, liberal education... critical discernment, delicate tact, disinterestedness, unsuspected morals, notorious patriotism, and tried Maecenasship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restoring classical or high standards in theatre, prefer managers with cultural authority and independence from mercenary motives rather than purely commercial managers whose profit motive may compromise taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: On theft/borrowing in literary creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wieland's 'thefts' are praised as 'so exquisitely managed, that the greatest writers might be proud to steal as he did'; old romance material is treated as a kind of common property to be used well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective borrowing or reworking of myths/romances can be legitimate if handled skillfully; evaluate such 'theft' by how artfully material is integrated and transformed.
